A threshold is only as good as the test behind it. lactater can compute 20 thresholds from any table of numbers,
but it cannot tell whether the athlete came to the test with empty glycogen stores, or whether the lactate was
sampled from the fingertip in one test and the earlobe in the next. This article collects what the literature says
about running a step test and analyzing it, as a checklist.

Read it with its evidence in mind. Few of these points come from guidelines: most come from single studies in small
groups, often of trained men, and some from expert reviews. Each point names its source, says when only the abstract
was read, and says so when no study was found.

## Before the test: the same athlete every time

The aim is that the only thing that differs between two tests is fitness.

* **Diet and glycogen.** Keep the diet of the 24 to 48 h before the test the same for every test, and avoid
  exercise that empties the glycogen stores. Low glycogen lowers lactate at every intensity and moves the curve to
  the right, which looks like better endurance (Maassen & Busse, 1989, abstract; Faude et al., 2009, review).
* **Training before the test.** Plan a day without hard training before each test, as the reliability study of
  Pallarés et al. (2016) did.
* **Caffeine.** Keep caffeine habits the same. In 8 men, 5 mg/kg of caffeine raised lactate at submaximal
  intensities and lowered the threshold at 2 mmol/L, while the breakpoint, the 1 mmol/L rise and the 4 mmol/L
  thresholds did not change (Gaesser & Rich, 1985, abstract).
* **Hydration.** In 7 moderately trained women, losing 2.6% of body mass to dehydration moved the lactate threshold
  from 72% to 66% of VO2max (Moquin & Mazzeo, 2000, abstract).
* **Time of day.** Test at the same time of day. In 11 trained rowers, oxygen uptake and heart rate at the Dmax
  threshold followed a circadian rhythm; the authors advise testing at the time the athlete usually trains (Forsyth &
  Reilly, 2004, abstract).
* **Warm-up and familiarization.** Use the same light warm-up every time, and let a new athlete do one
  familiarization test (Pallarés et al., 2016).

## The protocol

* **Stage duration.** Shorter stages put the thresholds at higher intensities, and stages of at least 3 min have
  been recommended (Bentley et al., 2007; Jamnick et al., 2020, both reviews; Jamnick et al., 2018, compared stages
  from 1 to 10 min). Whatever you choose, keep the protocol identical between tests of the same athlete:
  `compare_tests()` notes when it differs.
* **Number of stages.** No guideline sets a number. Six or more is common (Grant et al. 2002 used at least six 4-min
  stages), and lactater needs at least five for Log-log and six for two lactate turn points.
* **Start and increment.** Start low enough for two or three stages below the first rise in lactate: the methods for
  LT1 need them, and Dmax depends on where the test starts and ends (Jamnick et al., 2020).
* **End of the test.** Go to exhaustion when you use methods that rely on the last stage (the Dmax family and LTP2),
  because they change with the final lactate (Bentley et al., 2007; Jamnick et al., 2020). If the athlete stopped
  during the last stage, enter its time-weighted intensity, or leave it out with `max_intensity`.
* **Treadmill grade.** A 1% grade matched the energy cost of outdoor running in 9 trained runners (Jones & Doust,
  1996, abstract). Whatever the grade, keep it the same.
* **Pauses for sampling.** Short pauses to take the sample are common on a treadmill (Dickhuth et al. 1999 used
  30 s); keep them the same between tests.

## Taking the sample

* **Timing.** Sample in the last 30 s of each stage, as most studies do (Goodwin et al., 2007; Morton et al., 2012;
  Forsyth & Reilly, 2004).
* **Site.** Use the same site in every test. Values from the fingertip and the earlobe differ:
  * finger values were higher than earlobe and venous values on a cycle ergometer and a treadmill in 312 trained
    athletes, and the authors preferred the earlobe (Dassonville et al., 1998, abstract);
  * fingertip and earlobe differed by 9.2% on average in cycling, with 95% of differences between -25% and +59%
    (Moran et al., 2012);
  * the fingertip read 0.66 mmol/L higher than the earlobe in double poling on a ski ergometer (Zhong et al., 2025,
    abstract, 40 students);
  * fingertip, toe and earlobe did not differ significantly after rowing in 9 rowers (Forsyth & Farrally, 2000,
    abstract).
* **Skin preparation and hygiene.** Wear gloves, clean the site with 70% alcohol and let it dry in the air, wipe away
  the first drop of blood, do not squeeze hard, and put the lancet straight into a sharps container (World Health
  Organization, 2010). No study we found measured how much sweat on the skin changes a sample; drying the site is the
  usual advice.
* **Sample type.** Plasma lactate was about 50% higher than lactate in red blood cells, and capillary and venous
  whole blood also differed (Foxdal et al., 1990, 10 healthy men); whole-blood lactate is about 70% of plasma lactate,
  depending on the hematocrit (Goodwin et al., 2007, review). Never mix sample types between tests, and report which
  one you used (`sample` in `lactate_threshold()`). The fixed concentrations of OBLA, Bsln+ and IAT were defined on
  blood, so `lactate_checks()` warns when `sample` says otherwise.
* **Analyzer.** Calibrate it as the manufacturer says, and test each athlete on the same device. The typical error
  of three portable analyzers was 0.4 to 1.0 mmol/L depending on the device (Tanner et al., 2010, abstract), and
  six hand-held analyzers all read lower than a laboratory analyzer, most at the highest concentrations, which
  "would overestimate the ability of the athlete" (Bonaventura et al., 2015).

## What else to record

* **Heart rate and RPE** at the end of every stage, in the same window as the blood sample. For RPE, read the
  standard instructions before the test, ask for how hard the effort feels (not pain), and ask at the same moment of
  every stage (Lamb et al., 1999, abstract, asked in the last 15 s of 3-min stages). Give lactater the columns with
  `heart_rate_column`, `rpe_column` and `rpe_scale` (`"6-20"` or `"CR10"`).
* **Expect HR and RPE to vary.** The test-retest limits of agreement of RPE were about +/-2 to +/-3 units and widened
  as intensity rose (Lamb et al., 1999, 16 male athletes), and heart rate and RPE at the thresholds reproduced poorly
  between two tests (Grant et al., 2002, abstract). In 2,560 adults, RPE was 10.8 at the lactate threshold, 13.6 at
  the individual anaerobic threshold and 14.1 at 4 mmol/L (Scherr et al., 2013, abstract): a rough check, not a
  target.
* **The conditions**: room temperature and humidity, the ergometer and its settings, the athlete's diet and
  training in the days before. No study is needed for this one: without it, you cannot tell later why two tests
  differ.

Here is a simulated test with heart rate and RPE (the RPE of the simulated tests in `lactate_tests` is simulated
too):

```{r}
client <- subset(lactate_tests, test == "untrained")
client[c("intensity", "lactate", "heart_rate", "rpe")]
results <- lactate_threshold(
  client, intensity, lactate, heart_rate,
  rpe_column = "rpe", rpe_scale = "6-20", sample = "blood", plot = FALSE
)
results[results$method %in% c("Log-log", "LTP1", "LTP2", "OBLA 4.0"), c("method", "intensity", "heart_rate", "rpe")]
```

## Analyzing the test

* **Choose the methods and the curve before you look at the data**, and report them. Two methods can put the
  threshold of the same athlete about 30% apart (Jamnick et al., 2020), and no curve fit is generally accepted
  (Faude et al., 2009). [The methods article](methods.html) summarizes the evidence for each method.
* **Look at the data before trusting a number.** Plot the test, read `lactate_checks()`, and check how well the curve
  follows the stages and how much each threshold rests on one stage with `lactate_diagnostics()` (see [Checking
  the analysis](checking.html)).
* **Report how sure you are.** The precision of a threshold should be known before a change is called real (Bentley
  et al., 2007). `ci = TRUE` adds confidence intervals.
* **Know the noise of your own tests.** The typical error is the standard deviation of the test-retest differences
  divided by the square root of 2, best given as a coefficient of variation (Hopkins, 2000). It depends on the
  method and the study: Dmax had a standard error of measurement of 2.5 W against 9 to 25 W for other markers in 11
  fit adults tested at least six times (Morton et al., 2012, abstract), but a coefficient of variation of 10.3%
  against about 3% for the fixed and baseline methods in 14 trained cyclists (Pallarés et al., 2016). Measure it on
  your athletes with your protocol and give it to `compare_tests()` as `cv`.
* **Compare like with like.** Keep the protocol, the site, the sample type, the analyzer, the methods and the curve
  the same between tests of the same athlete. See [Comparing tests](compare.html).

## A checklist for your report

* Who was tested: sport, sex, age, training status.
* What happened before the test: diet, training, caffeine, time of day.
* The protocol: ergometer, start, increment, stage duration, pauses, how the test ended.
* The sample: site, timing within the stage, sample type, analyzer.
* The analysis: the methods and how they are defined (for the Dmax family, where the line starts and ends), the
  fitted curve, whether the resting sample was used, the software and its version (`packageVersion("lactater")`).
* The uncertainty: confidence intervals, and the typical error used to judge changes.
